subject: Application - Senior Platform Engineer (SRE), Western Europe Remote
paragraphs: I am applying for the Senior Platform Engineer (SRE) role. A platform whose users are its own engineers, run by one person who built it from nothing and wants a peer rather than a report, is close to the last four years of my own work: a fleet I designed, built and am still paged by, where the measure of the platform is that other engineers never have to ask me for a host. Being the second person on that team, with half a roadmap to own, is the shape of job I have been doing alone.

The operational half is what I would bring first. One flake declares thirteen NixOS hosts, with an SSH certificate authority, SOPS-encrypted secrets and a task interface as the only operator surface, so infrastructure is defined in code and reviewed like product code rather than clicked into existence. A sentinel writes job status, generation age, disk and pressure-stall figures to a ledger every fifteen minutes and pages when a state is not ok; alert noise is treated as a defect to remove rather than a cost of doing business, which is the discipline your on-call section describes. The services on it are Go and Python, a PostgreSQL-backed mail archive among them, and the security work is continuous in the same way: no shared user keys, age-key rotation for secrets, and a vulnerability programme built from CISA's KEV catalogue that orders patching by exposure and effort instead of severity score alone. That is the posture SOC 2 asks you to keep rather than sprint for.

The honest gaps are the tools. I have not run Kubernetes in production: my hosts are single-tenant and separated by role, and the isolation I have built is a certificate authority and a module boundary rather than namespaces, quotas and network policy, so the scheduler would be new ground rather than familiar. Terraform, Terragrunt and Helm are not in my hands either — my infrastructure-as-code is Nix, which reconciles a whole machine from a declared state, so the model is not foreign, but I would be learning your tools rather than arriving fluent in them. Kafka, Temporal and fifteen petabytes of object storage are scale I have not operated; my storage work is a NAS taxonomy, restic backups and media-tree isolation on hardware I own. And AWS in my history is a handful of instances, not a multi-region architecture I designed.

I am in south-west Germany, so Western Europe remote needs no relocation and no permit from me: I hold German permanent residence and work here without restriction, and CET sits inside your European spread for a shared pager. The Bring Your Own Storage problem is the part I would most want to argue about, because egress economics deciding whether sharing media is viable is a cost-and-reliability trade-off with numbers attached, and I have spent years on systems where those two pull against each other. I would welcome a conversation about which half of the roadmap I would take first, and about what I would need to learn fastest.
